newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian cen bank share speculators seen suffering.
newsitem.headline: Belgian cen bank share speculators seen suffering.

text.p: Speculators in the Belgian National Bank will soon find themselves sitting on shares that no one else wants to own, analysts said on Friday.
The shares go ex-dividend on February 26 and this will probably signal the end of a rally that has pushed them up to record levels this year -- levels they are unlikely to reach again any time soon.
"On the basis of a dividend discount model...the share should be worth 43,288 Belgian francs," BBL banking analyst Tony De Poortere told Reuters.
The BNB was trading at 60,500 francs in late Friday dealings, up 1,500 on the day.

A combination of rumours of a state-run share buyback and the prospect of the bank's 1996 dividend recently pushed the share up to a record 65,000 francs -- 25 percent more than at the start of the year, compared with an 11 percent rise in the Bel-20 leading share index.
But finance ministry and central bank officials say the buyback story is groundless and the bank's 1996 net dividend of 1,740 francs is due to be paid on March 1.

Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told Reuters on February 17 that to his knowledge there were no plans for the government to buy back the 50 percent of shares in the central bank that it does not already own.
That declaration helped knock the share off its high down to levels around 58,000 francs, but it has been moving back up steadily since in an otherwide downward market.

One trader said the prospect of a single European currency and associated European System of Central Banks meant some investors still held out hope of getting a bigger slice of the bank's future profits or asset sales.
A central bank spokesman said, however, the rumours were "nonsense".
"How is this possible?" he said, noting a draft law to bring the BNB's statutes in line with the requirements of the Maastricht Treaty proposed no change in how the bank shares out its profits.

Analysts agreed. "It's a stock which, on the basis of its price/book value per share, could be interesting. But because it's held by the state any capital gains it generates, such as the recent gold sales, go to the government," said Martine Deroamme of Generale Bank.
"We think it's time to sell if you still have it in your portfolio," she added.
Belgium's constitutional advisory body is expected to give its opinion on the draft central bank law in the coming days, after which it will begin its passage through parliament.
One informed source said, however, the so-called Conseil d'Etat had so far made only technical changes to the law. The chapters on the share-out of profits were expected to remain unchanged.
The law states that all capital gains made by the bank since January 1, 1987, notably from the sale of gold, go to the state.
Under the law, the state will also get all of the Belgian National Bank's share of the profit made by a future European Central Bank.
The draft law also states that the bank's annual general meeting of shareholders, due to be held next Monday, "does not have any possibility, in law or fact, to influence the policies of the bank."

The Belgian National Bank is one of the few listed European central banks. The others are the Swiss National Bank, whose shares can only be owned by Swiss nationals, and the Bank of Greece, whose share has also climbed rapidly since last year.
